title: Machinability and surface integrity evaluation of additive manufactured alloy 718 (PBF-LB) using binderless CBN and cemented carbide endmills
abstract: Abstract Additive manufactured (AM) offers significant design freedom for aerospace components, but many AM surfaces require machining to meet functional and dimensional requirements. Alloy 718 remains challenging to machine due to its high hot-hardness and strong work-hardening behaviour, and recent studies suggest that AM-induced microstructural variations may further influence machinability. This work compares the machinability with two solid end mill concepts, a cemented carbide tool and a binderless CBN (BL-CBN) tool, when machining Alloy 718 produced by Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB) in three material conditions: As-built, Hot Isostatic Pressed (HIP), heat-treated (AMS 5662) using a wrought Alloy 718 as reference. The comparison focuses on tool wear and surface integrity, including surface topography, residual stresses, and near-surface deformation. Machining tests were performed on small blade-shaped samples representative of a thin-walled aerospace component geometry. The results show clear differences in machinability between the two tool concepts. The cemented carbide tool is highly sensitive to the material condition, leading to higher surface roughness and lower compressive residual stresses compared to the BL-CBN tool. In contrast, the BL-CBN tool provides stable performance across all AM conditions. For the relatively short cutting lengths studied, machining-induced deformation remained low for both tools in the AM materials. However, wrought Alloy 718 material remains the most challenging material to machine, as it caused highest tool wear, deepest residual stresses and largest plastic deformation.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Additive manufacturing (AM) is growing across many industrial sectors, with particularly strong adoption in the medical, aviation and space industries [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. In the latter two sectors, nickel-based superalloys are widely used for engine components due their excellent high-temperature properties.

Among the various AM technologies, powder bed fusion using laser beam (PBF-LB) is one of the most established processes for metallic materials. In this method, thin layers of powder are spread across a build platform and selectively melted by the laser beam according to the CAD geometry, producing the component layer by layer [ 4 ]. The resulting microstructure is strongly influenced by the printing strategy and powder characteristics. In general, the rapid solidification inherent to the PBF-LB produces a fine hierarchical microstructure consisting of melt pools, cellular structures, and columnar grains aligned with the building direction [ 5 ,  6 ]. To further homogenise the microstructure and tailor the mechanical properties, various heat-treatment routes can be applied [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ]. These treatments often aim to dissolve and redistribute, segregated elements such as Ti, Al, and Nb, thereby reducing the Laves δ-phase formation and promoting precipitation of strengthening γ’ and γ’’ phases [ 10 ]. For example, Popovic et al. demonstrated that applying the AMS 5664E heat-treatment cycle transformed the as-built Laves-phase to δ-phase precipitates, resulting in improved fatigue performance [ 11 ].

Despite its design flexibility, PBF-LB also have some limitations. One of the most prominent is the relatively rough surface topography of as-built components, with arithmetic mean height (Sa) values typically ranging from 5 to 15 μm [ 12 ]. This roughness depends on several factors, including layer thickness, contour, laser power, laser speed, and build orientation [ 13 ,  14 – 15 ]. While such surfaces may be acceptable for non-critical features, most functional surfaces require a significantly lower roughness, making machining essential and a continued area for research.

From a machining perspective, conventional wrought Alloy 718 is already considered difficult to cut due to its high strength, strong work-hardening tendency, and low thermal conductivity, all of which promote heat accumulation and accelerated tool wear. These effects directly influence the resulting surface integrity [ 16 ,  17 ]. Machining additive manufactured Alloy 718 introduces additional complexity because the AM process imparts microstructural features that vary with build orientation and processing parameters, which is not observed in wrought condition [ 10 ]. These include columnar and fine-grain structures, varying porosity levels, and differences in type and distribution of precipitates, as reported by Marques et al. [ 6 ]. Numerous studies have investigated the tool-wear mechanism when machining wrought Alloy 718 using end mills [ 18 ,  19 – 20 ], generally recommending high cutting speeds and low depths of cut to mitigate excessive cutting temperatures. For AM alloy 718, Malakizadi et al. showed that the differences in microstructure constituents arising from various AM processes and post heat-treatment significantly affect work-hardening and, consequently, tool wear [ 21 ]. Furthermore, the amount, morphology, and distribution of precipitates have been shown to strongly influence both tool wear and surface quality [ 22 ]. Similar conclusions have been drawn for turning operations on AM Alloy 718 in both as-built and heat-treated conditions, where precipitate characteristics were identified as a dominant factor governing machinability [ 22 ].

Furthermore, when De Bartolomeis et al. reviewed machinability of both conventional and AM alloy 718, the authors highlighted several important distinctions. For conventional Alloy 718, cubic boron nitride (CBN) cutting tools are commonly used at significantly higher cutting speeds compared to carbide tools, enabling higher productivity but potentially affecting the resulting surface integrity [ 23 ]. Their review further noted that AM Alloy 718 generally exhibits lower hardness and higher ductility compared to conventional material. In addition, the strong anisotropy associated with the building direction in AM components can induce fluctuating thermomechanical loads on the cutting tool, suggesting that tools with high toughness, such as cemented carbide tools, may be advantageous. Another key challenge when machining AM Alloy 718 is its increased strain-hardening tendency, which arises from the heterogeneous microstructure and constituents distribution inherent to the AM processing [ 24 ].

Tool selection is therefore crucial when optimising machining performance for AM-produced materials, and a natural starting point is to consider machining of conventional wrought Alloy 718, which can be machined using a wide range of tools, including coated carbide, ceramic, or CBN tools [ 25 ]. The suitability of each tool grade depends on its thermal resistance, softening temperature, and the microstructure of the work piece material. As summarised by Kramer et al., CBN tools maintain significantly higher hot-hardness than cemented carbide and preserve their mechanical integrity at elevated temperatures [ 26 ]. Above these temperatures, tool degradation accelerates rapidly. Although cemented carbide tools can be tailored for specific performance through microstructure optimisation [ 27 ], CBN tools generally deliver higher overall performance but at a higher cost, which must be justified by corresponding gains in productivity [ 28 ,  29 ].

Understanding the surface and subsurface conditions of AM material prior to machining is therefore essential when selecting suitable cutting tools and parameters, as these factors directly influence achievable surface integrity, dimensional accuracy, and tool life. Despite the rapid advancement of AM technologies, the large number of process parameters and resulting variability in surface and subsurface characteristics urge increased knowledge regarding machinability of AM materials. This lack of understanding continues to constrain broader industrial adoption.

In this work, the surface integrity of machined AM Alloy 718 is evaluated and compared to machined conventional wrought Alloy 718 using two tool concepts: a solid cemented carbide end mill and a binderless CBN end mill. The binderless CBN tool has been specifically designed to improve productivity and surface integrity when machining AM Alloy 718 components. However, the machining parameters for both concepts have been developed for wrought material. Based on the existing literature, substantial differences in machinability between AM material and wrought material variants are expected. Therefore, the primary objective of this study is to clarify how machining response and resulting surface integrity differs between the AM Alloy 718 and wrought Alloy 718 when using the two tool concepts with their respective best practice machining parameters. The purpose was to investigate whether process parameters need to be further optimized for AM material.

sections.heading: Methodology
paragraphs: The objective of the study was to investigate how surface integrity and machinability were affected when applying the two different tool concepts, a cemented carbide tool and a binderless CBN (BL-CBN) tool, with their respective best practice machining settings on AM material in different conditions: as-built, Hot Isostatically Pressed (HIP), and heat-treated according to AMS 5662. These conditions were selected to represent the range of microstructures typically encountered in industrial AM workflows. Wrought material was used as a reference.
To achieve the objective, machining experiments were conducted and a number of evaluations were performed:

Tool wear was monitored and cutting forces were measured. Surface topography, and surface residual stresses were evaluated at defined cutting lengths. Residual stress depth profiles were determined after a selected cutting length for all conditions cut with either the CC tool or the CBN tool. The Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of the diffraction peak, hardness profiles and evaluation of the microstructure were used to assess the machining-induced plastic deformation.
Measurements were compared across the three AM conditions and the wrought reference material, to establish the influence of microstructure and tool concept on machinability and surface integrity.

sections.heading: Wrought reference material
paragraphs: A wrought Alloy 718 material in solution-annealed and aged condition, according to ASTM 670, was used as the reference material. After heat-treatment, the material exhibited a yield strength of 1120, an ultimate strength of 1432 MPa, and a hardness of 43 HRC. The chemical composition is provided in Table  1 . Due to limited access to test material and excessive tool wear, not all evaluations were possible to perform on the wrought material.

paragraphs: In total, 54 blade specimens were printed, along with 24 test cubes used for preliminary microstructural analyses of the as-built, heat-treated, and HIP conditions. The layout of the build plate and the blade geometry are shown in Fig.  1 . The printing parameters were selected based on recommendation from the machine supplier, SLM Solutions, as shown in Table  3 .

sections.heading: Hot isostatic pressing (HIP)
paragraphs: HIP is a widely used method to densify material with inherent porosity [ 30 ]. Modern HIP systems also combine the HIP cycle with heat treatment, which can significantly reduce the overall cycle time [ 18 ]. In this work, HIP was performed using a Quintus QIH15L URC ® /URQ ®  furnace in a combined heating and quenching cycle. An established HIP cycle was applied [ 31 ], with a total duration of 9 h, consisting of a 3-hour precipitation-hardening step followed by a 5-hour aging step, as illustrated by the temperature and pressure graphs in Fig.  2 . The detailed HIP parameters are provided in Table  4 .
Fig. 2 HIP temperature and pressure cycle

Table 4 HIP process settings Description Setting Unit Machine QIH 15 L URC ® /URQ ®  (60 L volume) HIP cycle recipe IN718 - Solution Heat-treatment [31] Cooling rate 116 °C/s Pressure 200, 128 during ageing MPa Gas Argon % Furnace Type Used Molybdenum URQ ®  (Uniform Rapid Quenching)

sections.heading: Heat-treatment (HT)
paragraphs: In addition to HIP processing, a conventional heat-treatment was performed in a vacuum furnace in accordance with AMS 5662. This treatment consisted of a solution step at 982 °C for 60 min, followed by two-step aging cycle at 720 °C and 621 °C for 480 min at each temperature. After the final aging step, the specimens were air-cooled to room temperature.

sections.heading: Machining settings
paragraphs: Machining of both the AM and wrought Alloy 718 samples was performed on a DMG MORI DMU 60 eVo linear machining centre equipped with a SumiForce sensing unit for cutting-force measurements. The study focused on evaluating the effect of using best-practice parameters for wrought Alloy 718 when applied to AM alloy 718. Thus, a different set of cutting parameters was used for each tool concept, and the cutting parameters were kept constant for each tool concept.

Tool concept 1: Solid cemented carbide (CC) ball-nose end mill, GSXB series, with 2 teeth and a radius of 4 mm. Tool concept 2: Binderless cubic boron (BL-CBN) ball-nose end mill, NCB100, with 4 teeth and a radius of 4 mm.

Prior to the experiments, the parts were pre-machined to remove the “black scale” using a GSX41200C-4D end mill with 4 teeth and a radius of 12 mm (clean cut). The cutting conditions used are summarised in Table  5 . A Yushiro FGE57 coolant was used in all tests.

Table 5 Machining settings used to machine the samples Tool/Setting Vc [m/min] (Rev/min) fz [mm/tooth] (mm/min) ap [mm] ae [mm] Coolant Strategy Clean cut 50 (1592) 0.05 (318) 20 0.1 Flood Down mill CC 50 (2000) 0.05 (200) 0.1 0.1 Flood Down mill BL-CBN 452 (18000) 0.02 (440) 0.1 0.1 MQL Down mill

The machining tests were performed using the setup shown in Fig.  3 , where the samples were tilted 30° relative to the tool engagement. The setup was based on standard test procedures used internally by the tool manufacturer to achieve representative machining conditions when evaluating new tools. Fig. 3 Machining setup for the cutting tests and force measurements directions

The lower part of each specimen was rigidly clamped to minimise vibration during machining. Cutting forces and tool wear (VB max ) were measured according to the tool-based coordinate system illustrated in Fig.  3  (right). Cutting forces were measured by a SumiForce sensing unit integrated into the tool holder and the cutting force directions are defined relative to the tool. Evaluations of the workpiece, such as for residual stresses, were measured separately from the machining according to the coordinate system shown in Fig.  3  (left). The feed direction is parallel between the two coordinates systems.

sections.heading: Surface integrity evaluation methods
paragraphs: Geometry of the parts was measured using an ATOS GOM II optical scanner with a measurement volume of 320 × 240 × 240 mm and a point spacing of 0.104 mm. The scanned geometry was compared to the CAD model using a best-fit alignment.

Surface topography was measured using a Sensofar S neox instrument. Prior to machining, measurements were made using the confocal fusion method [ 32 ]. Areas of 2.4 × 1.8 mm were measured at 20x magnification, with a lateral sampling of 0.65 μm. After machining, areas of 1.0 × 5.0 mm were measured using coherence scanning interferometry at 10x magnification, with a lateral sampling of 1.29 μm. The measured topography data were processed by form removal using a second-degree polynomial fit and filtered with a spatial median noise-reduction filter (window size of 5 × 5 points) to reduce short-wavelength noise, resulting in S-F surfaces for analysis. Surface texture parameters Sa (arithmetic mean height) and S10z (ten-point height) were calculated in accordance with ISO 25178-2:2021 [ 33 ].

Residual stresses were measured using X-ray diffraction with a G2R XStress 3000 system and Xtronic 1.13.2 software (Stresstech Oy). The system was equipped with a manganese X-ray source (λ:0.2103 nm) and a 2 mm collimator. The modified sin 2 χ method was applied using ten tilt angles in each direction (± 40°), measuring the (311) lattice plane at a diffraction angle of 151.88°, selected based on recommendation in SAE International HS-784 [ 34 ]. Stress calculations were based on elastic strain theory using Hooke’s law, with a Young’s modulus of 199.9 GPa and a Poisson’s ratio of 0.294. Measurements were performed in accordance with SS-EN 15305:2008 [ 35 ]. Measurements were made in feed and across feed direction, as shown in Fig.  3  (left), as this is aligned with the principal stress directions.

Microstructure and hardness were evaluated on polished cross-sections using a Jeol LV6610 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with a Brucker XFlash 5010 energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detector. The grain size was estimated by counting the number of grain boundaries intersected along three vertical and three horizontal lines in each micrograph. Hardness was measured using a Qness Q10 A+ hardness tester. Cross-sections were taken along the feed direction to reveal the microstructural features relevant to the machining process. The bulk hardness was measured at a depth of 2–6 mm below the surface using the average of six indents per sample. The deformation depth was estimated based on five measurements of the deformed surface microstructure in each of the representative micrographs for each condition.

sections.heading: Material prior to machining
paragraphs: The surface and bulk microstructures of the materials prior to machining are shown in Fig.  4 . The wrought material exhibits randomly oriented grains with sizes in the range of 20–50 μm. In contrast, the AM material displays a columnar grain structure near the surface, with grains aligned along the building direction, while the bulk region contains more randomly oriented but extended grains.
Fig. 4 Surface and bulk micrographs for the four different material conditions

The shape, size and distribution of precipitation and Laves-phase constituents in the three AM material conditions were further examined, as shown in Fig.  5 . Clear differences were observed between the samples in terms of the type, amount and distribution of precipitates. The as-built material formed a heterogeneous Nb- and Mo-rich Lavas-phase network. The columnar network structure is confined within each grain and becomes wider near the surface compared to the bulk. In contrast, the HIP-processed material contains only a few spherical δ-phase precipitates located primarily at the grain boundaries. The dark features are Al- and Ti-enrichments, which are confined to the very outer surface. The heat-treated material shows almost complete dissolution of the Lavas phase into the matrix, accompanied by the formation of small needle-shaped δ-phase precipitates. These δ-phase features were more abundant in the bulk than near the surface.
Fig. 5 SEM micrographs of the three different AM material revealing the size/distribution of the precipitates in the surface and the bulk

The near-surface chemistry was investigated using EDS, as shown in Fig.  6 . The results revealed elevated levels of Ti and O for the HIP and heat-treated samples, indicating the presence of a surface oxidation layer, as shown in Fig.  6 . The oxide thickness was estimated to be approximately 2 μm. This surface oxide layer showed that the alloying elements had migrated to the surface, resulting in a Cr-rich outermost layer followed by a Mo- and Nb-rich subsurface region.
Fig. 6 Near the surface SEM/EDS maps of the three material conditions, revealing the amount and shape of the hard delta phase precipitates and diffusion of elements towards the surface

The bulk hardness for the different samples is presented in Table  6 . The as-built material exhibited a bulk hardness of 310 HV1, whereas both the HIP and heat-treated samples showed an approximate hardness increase of 58%. Table 6 Bulk hardness and evaluation of grain size, mean values with standard deviations Sample Hardness, HV1 [kgf/mm 2 ] Grain size in build direction [µm] Grain size in across building direction [µm] Wrought 459 ± 8 30 ± 10 As-built 310 ± 10 40.8 ± 10.3 17.6 ± 2.1 HIP 478 ± 11 44.9 ± 7.7 21.3 ± 1.7 HT 480 ± 9 65.0 ± 21.1 28.3 ± 4.3

Grain size was evaluated on the cross-section of the test cubes in both the build direction and the transverse direction. Weld lines were clearly visible in the as-built condition but could not be resolved in the HIP or heat-treated samples, indicating dissolution of the melt-pool boundaries during thermal processing. The results of the grain size evaluation are shown in Table  6 . The HIPed samples exhibited a larger grain size compared to the as-built condition, while the heat-treated samples shows a significantly coarser grain structure. In all AM conditions, the grains size in building directions was approximately twice the size measured in transverse direction. The melt-pool width in the as-built samples was approximately 0.2 mm.

sections.heading: Machining tests
paragraphs: The cutting forces in the tool-axis direction (F Z  max and F Z  average) and the in-plane force component (F X−Y  max and F X−Y  average) are presented in Figs.  7  and  8 , with the coordinate directions defined in Fig.  3  (right). Measurements from passes 1–5 are shown as solid-coloured bars and passes 396–400 as shaded bars with dashed lines in each diagram. The maximum measured force values are shown to the left (A) and the average values to the right (B). As expected, the along tool-axis cutting forces, F Z , are substantially higher than the in-plane forces, F X−Y . Fig. 7 Maximum cutting forces for (A) F Z  (tool axis direction) and (B) F X−Y  (in-plane direction) at different cutting passes 1–5 and 396–400 for the three different AM material conditions Fig. 8 Average cutting forces for (A) F Z  (tool axis direction) and (B) F X−Y  (in-plane direction) at different cutting passes 1–5 and 396–400 for the three different AM material conditions

The results show that the cemented carbide tool generated significantly higher maximum cutting forces compared to the BL-CBN tool, approximately three times higher in both the HIP and heat-treated conditions. It is further observed that, for all cases with cemented carbide, the maximum cutting forces increase with the number of passes, in both F Z  and F X−Y  components, Fig.  7  (A) and (B). The cemented carbide tool exhibited a substantial variation in maximum F z  cutting force between the different material conditions, also observed for the in-plane force component F X−Y . On the other hand, the BL-CBN tool shows relatively consistent cutting forces for both F z  and F Z−Y , with only a slight increase across the three material conditions, although a noticeable increase is observed when comparing the initial passes with the final passes.

The corresponding average cutting forces are presented in Fig.  8 . These results show lower magnitudes and a different behaviour compared to the maximum forces. F z  shows higher forces with an increasing number of passes for the BL-CBN tool, but comparably similar values for all three conditions, while the cemented carbide tool show a significant increase in forces for the heat-treated condition. For the in-plane forces, F X−Y , both tools show similar magnitudes consistently across all three material conditions.

Tool wear was mainly observed on the flank face, with a consistent worn area most apparent on the CC tool, as shown in Fig.  9 . No abnormal tool damage, such as chipping, was observed. Hence, VBmax was used as the most representative parameter to describe the tool wear.
Fig. 9 Tool wear for wrought material of the two inserts at different spiral cutting lengths (SCL), flank wear marked with yellow arrows

Figure  10  shows the tool-wear progression, represented by VBmax, for the two studied tools after machining in the four different material conditions. The results indicate that the tool wear of the cemented carbide tool is greatly influenced by the material condition, whereas the BL-CBN exhibits consistently lower wear progression across all conditions, with only a small offset between them.
Fig. 10 Tool wear, VB max, versus cutting length for the two tools and four material conditions, error bars represent the max and min measures of the VB over the different cutting edges

The wrought material resulted in significantly higher wear for both tool concepts, highest for the cemented carbide tool, but no notch wear was observed for either of the tools in the tested cutting length interval. However, the cemented carbide tool exhibited a pronounced wear zone even after the relatively short cutting length of 32 m. In contrast, the BL-CBN tool showed only minor wear after 288 m cutting length. The corresponding wear when machining the AM material was minimal for both tools in comparison.

sections.heading: Topography
paragraphs: The visual appearance and corresponding 3D geometry of the test samples are shown in Fig.  11 . A clear visual difference is observed: the as-built sample show a metallic, shiny surface, whereas the HIP- and heat-treated samples are discoloured due to surface oxidation. The coloured 3D-geometry maps illustrate the deviation from the CAD model, where green indicate a good fit, blue represents undersized regions, and red denotes oversized areas. The as-built sample appears to be close to the nominal dimensions, whereas the HIP and heat-treated samples are distorted, mainly at the tip of the specimen. However, the distortions are small (in the range of 30–40 μm), which indicates limited internal stresses.
Fig. 11 Overview of the samples for the three different AM material conditions

The surface topography of the AM samples prior to machining is shown in Fig.  12 . The surface has a wavy appearance with smooth hills, and the surfaces are covered with small, unmelted powder particles. The results indicate that all samples exhibit similar surface characteristics, with Sa values in the range of 5.5–6.1 μm and S10z values between 61 and 107 μm, which are mean values of six different samples measured at three positions on each.
Fig. 12 3D topography maps and parameters  before machining  of the three AM material conditions

The surface topography of the four material conditions after machining is shown in Fig.  13 , with corresponding extracted profiles across feed direction presented in Fig.  14 . A clear difference is observed between the two tool concepts: the cemented carbide tool produced a pronounced long-wavelength waviness, whereas the BL-CBN tool generated no long-wavelength waviness but a slightly higher short-wavelength roughness, which is clearly apparent when comparing the profiles.
Fig. 13 3D topography maps and parameters  after machining  of the four material conditions
Fig. 14 Profiles and parameters  after machining  of the four material conditions. Mean values with standard deviations from ten profiles exacted from each surface

The evolution of surface roughness with cutting length is shown in Fig.  15 . The results clearly demonstrates that the cemented carbide tool is strongly affected by the material condition, whereas the BL-CBN tool produces similar roughness regardless of the material. The CC tool yields the highest surface roughness when machining the HIP material, while the as-built material exhibits significantly lower Sa values, comparable to those for all material conditions machined with the BL-CBN tool. For the wrought material, only two measurement points were available, both indicating a decrease in surface roughness at the longest cutting length, attributed to progressive tool wear.
Fig. 15 Arithmetic mean height (Sa) and ten point height (S10z) for different cutting lengths (CL) in the four material conditions

sections.heading: Residual stress
paragraphs: The surface residual stresses after machining at different cutting lengths (CL) are shown in Fig.  16 . These measurements were performed on different samples, required to reach the different cutting lengths, but at the same position in the centre of the samples. The initial stress state varies considerably between the material conditions, with the as-built material exhibiting high tensile stresses, the HIP material showing compressive stresses, and the heat-treated material displaying stresses close to zero. After machining, all materials show an initial rapid increase in compressive stress, and at longer cutting lengths the stress levels converge. Overall, both cutting tools induced compressive stresses for all material conditions. Fig. 16 Surface residual stresses after machining for different cutting length (CL) and material conditions with ( A ) Cemented carbide (CC) tool and ( B ) BL-CBN tool. Error bars represent the deviation from linear fitting of the diffraction data when using the sin 2 ψ method

The cemented carbide tool shows large variations in stress magnitude between the different conditions, with highest compressive stresses for the HIP material. For the BL-CBN tool, all AM conditions coincide around approximately − 600 MPa, except for the as-built material in the feed direction. The wrought material generally shows low stresses close to zero; however, at the CL 256 m the stresses shift drastically to tensile stresses in feed direction. This abrupt change suggests a significant alteration in tool condition, likely chipping, which is consistent with the corresponding surface topography data.

The residual stress depth profiles were measured at a common cutting length of 96 m for all four material conditions, as shown in Fig.  17  for feed direction and across-feed direction in Fig.  18 . In feed direction, the as-built and heat-treated materials machined with cemented carbide tools exhibit similar profiles, characterised by low compressive surface stress and a shallow affected depth. The HIP material shows substantially higher compressive stresses for the same tool, and, unlike the other AM conditions, the stress profile remains compressive throughout the measured depths. The wrought material machined with the CC tool shows low compressive surface stresses that increase with depth, resulting in the greatest overall impact depth among the materials. Fig. 17 Residual stresses after machining (CL: 96 m) in  Feed direction  for the four material conditions with ( A ) Cemented carbide (CC) tool and ( B ) BL-CBN tool. Error bars represent the deviation from linear fitting of the diffraction data when using the sin 2 ψ method Fig. 18 Residual stresses after machining (96 m) in  Across feed direction  for the four material conditions with ( A ) Cemented carbide (CC) tool and ( B ) BL-CBN tool. Error bars represent the deviation from linear fitting of the diffraction data when using the sin 2 ψ method

For the BL-CBN tool, the results differentiate the material conditions more distinctly. The as-built material shows the lowest compressive surface stress and the shallowest impact depth. The HIP and heat-treated materials exhibit similar surface stress levels, but their profiles diverge at greater depth due to difference in inherent stress states. The wrought material presents high compressive surface stresses that transition into tensile stress at greater depths, with the deepest total impact, extending to approximately 0.15 mm.

In the across-feed direction, the two tools also exhibit slight differences in residual stress profiles. For both tools, the surface stresses are compressive. For the CC tool with the heat-treatment and HIP samples, there is a change into low tensile stresses in the bulk, whereas the BL-CBN tool produces stresses close to zero in this region. In contrast, the as-built sample shows high tensile stresses in the bulk, approaching the same magnitudes measured prior to machining, as indicated by the light grey coloured reference profiles.

sections.heading: Microstructure and hardness
paragraphs: The near-surface microstructure after machining is shown in Fig.  19 . The two tool concepts produce similar types of surface impact, but the extent and character of the deformation vary between the material conditions. The as-built material shows deformation primarily in the form of grain refinement, with a slightly deeper affected zone for the BL-CBN tool, as indicated by the dashed yellow lines. In contrast, the HIP material shows deformation dominated by material drag, with the deepest impact observed for the CC tool. The heat-treated material displays a shallow deformation zone characterised by a combined deformation of material drag and grain refinement. Fig. 19 Micrographs from cross sections of the machined (96 m) surfaces for the two tools and the four material conditions, dashed lines and numbers represent the estimated deformation depth

Clear differences in microstructural constitution are also observed, particularly in the distribution of precipitates. The as-built material contains a high amount of cellular white Laves-phase, oriented and arranged within each grain. The HIP samples, however, show a predominantly austenitic structure with no obvious precipitates present; it is possible that these precipitates are too small to be resolved at this magnification. The heat-treated microstructure contains a high amount of fine, needle-shaped δ-phase precipitates that are randomly distributed throughout the matrix.

The hardness profiles for the blade samples after a cutting length of 96 m are presented in Fig.  20 . Consistent with the hardness of the test cube specimens, the as-built material exhibits significantly lower hardness compared to the HIP and heat-treated materials. The profiles show no clear evidence of surface softening or deformation hardening induced by the machining. For both the as-built and HIP materials, the hardness profiles are similar regardless of the tool used. In contrast, the heat-treated material displays an offset, with higher hardness for the samples machined using the CC tool.
Fig. 20 Hardness profiles after machining (96 m) with CC and BL-CBN tools of the four material conditions

Diffraction peak broadening (FWHM) provides an indication of the degree of plastic deformation introduced during machining and therefore serves as a useful measure when comparing different machining concepts [ 36 ]. The left graph in Fig.  21  presents the surface FWHM values for different cutting lengths when using CC tool, whiles the right graph shows the FWHM for the BL-CBN tool after various cutting lengths. Fig. 21 Surface FHWM versus cutting length for ( A ) Cemented carbide tool and ( B ) BL-CBN tool for the four material conditions

The surface FWHM results reveals more pronounced differences between the tools, with the CC tool producing lowest FWHM values in the as-built and heat-treated conditions compared to the BL-CBN tool. Although the initial FWHM values vary slightly between the material conditions, the values stabilize after a cutting length of 32 m.

The FWHM depth profiles show a greater variation between the material conditions for the CC tool than for the BL-CBN tool at a cutting length of 96 m, as shown in Fig.  22 . For the CC tool, the wrought material displays the highest FWHM values, while the as-built material shows the lowest. In contrast, the profiles for the BL-CBN tool coincides, demonstrating similar behaviour across all material conditions, with a total affected depth of approximately 30 μm.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The selection of machining concepts can be a difficult task for new material grades, especially when it comes to additive manufactured materials that tend to have complex microstructures. This has a direct impact on the machinability and surface integrity of the workpiece. Hence, traditional tool concepts and machining strategies may need to be further developed to work optimally. In this respect, a machinability evaluation comparing two different machining concepts has been carried out to investigate differences in how the machinability and workpiece surface integrity is affected when machining wrought and AM Alloy 718.

Firstly, a direct comparison of the two cutting tools in this work is not possible since each of the selected tools requires specific machining parameters. In this case, a much higher cutting speed is used for BL-CBN, resulting in higher productivity [ 23 ]. Another difference in this case is that the BL-CBN tool has four cutting edges whereas the cemented carbide tool has two cutting edges. This may influence both the surface topography and the wear, as the load is distributed over a different number of cutting edges. However, from an industrial perspective, it is interest to investigate how the established best practice approach, the CC tool concept, responds to cutting in AM materials, as well as to compare it with an alternative approach using a BL-CBN tool concept.

There are a number of potential random and systematic errors that may influence the measured surface integrity aspects in this work. One of the main sources of random errors arises from local microstructural variations within the DED-LB/p deposits, causing local variations in microstructure or small fluctuations in the strain response between measurement points. Systematic errors related to residual stress measurements may stem from instrument calibration, surface preparation, or assumptions in the measurement methods, particularly the use of material constants that may not fully represent the anisotropic, process-affected AM alloy. Pre-existing stresses in the substrate or incomplete stress relief after heat-treatment may also bias the results. While these uncertainties may affect the absolute stress magnitudes, the relative trends observed between the different material conditions remain robust. These concerns are further discussed in Sect.  4.5 .

sections.heading: Influence of AM material condition on microstructure and hardness
paragraphs: The three AM material conditions exhibit pronounced microstructure differences, which strongly influence their mechanical response and machinability. The as-built material contains a heterogeneous network of Nb- and Mo-rich Laves-phase, arranged in a cellular structure within each grain. The HIP process dissolved most of the Lavas-phase, resulting in a predominant austenite matrix with only a few small grain-boundary precipitates. Heat-treatment transform the Laves-phase into a high density of fine, needle-shaped δ-delta phase and strengthening γ’/γ’’ precipitates distributed throughout the matrix. The observed microstructures align with those reported in other works [ 5 ,  6 ,  23 ].

These microstructural differences are reflected through the hardness measurements. The as‑built condition shows significantly lower hardness, while both HIP and heat‑treated materials exhibit an approximate 60% increase. For these two materials, the substantially higher hardness align with the established relationship between homogenisation, δ-phase precipitation, and mechanical strengthening [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ]. The hardness profiles of the machined blades confirm this trend and show no evidence of machining‑induced softening or hardening, indicating that the machining parameters did not significantly alter the bulk microstructure.

The main differences between the AM material and the wrought material lie in the microstructural texture and distribution and size of different phases. The wrought material has an austenitic grain structure with randomly oriented grains with an average size of 20–50 μm, along with large δ-phase precipitates at the grain boundaries. A microstructure that is as expected and reported by others [ 10 ]. These precipitates are the result of the precipitation hardening process, which can be further optimised to reduce grain size to lower the impact on tool wear. This represents a significant difference compared to the columnar texture in the AM material, which arise from the printing process. The distribution, shape and size of the precipitates have a great impact on the material hardness and consequently the tool wear.

sections.heading: Cutting forces and tool wear mechanisms
paragraphs: The cutting-force measurements revealed a strong dependence on both tool material and AM material condition. The cemented carbide tool consistently generated much higher cutting forces, up to three times higher, than the BL-CBN tool, particularly for the HIP and heat-treated materials. The higher cutting forces for the two harder materials contradicts the results presented by Malakizadi et al., who showed slightly lower cutting forces when machining heat-treated LB-PBF material (aged and solution treated) compared to the as-built condition [ 21 ]. This suggests that the differences could be attributed to different tool design, indicating its influence. The higher cutting forces are attributed to the higher hardness and strength of these material conditions, which increase the mechanical load on the cutting edge, also reported in the literature for wrought Alloy 718 [ 16 ,  17 ].

The BL-CBN tool maintains stable cutting forces across all AM conditions, reflecting better hot-hardness and thermal resistance of the CBN tools, in line with reports by Kramer and De Bartolomeis [ 23 ,  26 ]. In contrast, the CC tools exhibits a substantial increase of cutting forces with increasing cutting length, especially for the harder HIP and heat-treated materials, consistent with accelerated wear mechanisms for cemented carbide tools described by others [ 18 ,  19 – 20 ].

Tool wear observations support these explanations, as the CC tool exhibits severe wear even at short cutting lengths in the wrought material and significant wear in the AM conditions. In contrast, the BL-CBN tool maintained low wear across all AM materials, with only minor differences between conditions. The wrought material induced the highest wear for both tools, highlighting its poorer machinability compared to the AM variants. This is most likely due to the presence of larger hard phases in the material, along with greater microstructural variation, such as large grain size.

The main reason for this outcome is believed to be the higher thermal conductivity of BL-CBN compared to cemented carbide, which leads to reduction in thermally induced degrading effects in the tool. The higher thermal conductivity lowers the temperatures in the cutting zone and thereby reduces tool wear and the negative impact on surface integrity.

Although a difference could be expected between the two tool concepts, since the CC tool only has two cutting edges while the BL-CBN has four, which doubles the amount of wear per edge on the CC tool, the wear progression is still much higher for the CC tool. This is linked to how the tool responds to the amount and distribution of the hard precipitates. Additionally, micro-geometry differences between the tool concepts provides different conditions for cutting forces and the tool wear.

Developing an underlying mechanistic explanation was not the objective of the present work. However, this work clearly identified that acquiring such understanding requires in-depth microstructural investigations at much higher resolution, using techniques like EBSD, scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), or atom probe analysis of representative samples from the machined surfaces. It is further believed that the interaction between the cutting edge of the tool and the microstructural constitution of the material plays an important role in both the tool wear and the resulting surface integrity, which will be addressed in future research.

sections.heading: Surface topography and residual stress state after machining
paragraphs: Prior to machining, all AM samples exhibited similar surface topographies, with Sa values ranging from 6 to 7 μm, which are typical values for this type of surface [ 11 ,  12 – 13 ]. After machining, the two tool concepts produce distinct surface characteristics. The CC tool generates a long‑wavelength texture, while the BL‑CBN tool produces a short‑wavelength texture with slightly higher amplitude but with no large‑scale waviness. This could be attributed to a combination of differences related to number of cutting edges, cutting parameters, radial run-out, and tool stiffness, with the BL-CBN tool appearing to be more robust.

The evolution of surface roughness with cutting length further highlights the sensitivity of the CC tool to the material condition. The HIP material yields the highest roughness, consistent with its higher hardness and reduced ductility after homogenisation [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ]. The as‑built material shows much lower Sa values, comparable to those obtained with the BL‑CBN tool, reflecting lower hardness and more ductile microstructure of the workpiece material [ 6 ,  22 ]. The BL‑CBN tool produces consistent roughness across all conditions, reflecting its stable performance.

The initial residual stress states differ markedly between the AM conditions: high tensile stresses in the as‑built material due to the rapid solidification [ 5 ,  6 ], compressive stresses in the HIP material due to stress relaxation [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ], and near‑zero stresses in the heat‑treated material, which is in agreement with other studies [ 12 ].

Machining introduces compressive stresses in all cases, with stress levels converging at longer cutting lengths. This also follows the machining-induced deformation mechanism for nickel-based superalloys described in the literature [ 14 ,  15 ]. The CC tool produces large variations in stress magnitudes between material conditions, with the HIP material showing the highest compressive stresses. The BL‑CBN tool generates more uniform compressive stresses around − 600 MPa for all AM conditions, except for the as‑built material in the feed direction.

Depth‑profile measurements at a cutting length of 96 m reveal that the HIP material retains compressive stresses throughout the measured depth when machined with the CC tool, whereas the as‑built and heat‑treated materials show shallow compressive layers. The wrought material exhibits the deepest impact, with compressive stresses transitioning to tensile stresses at greater depth.

For the BL‑CBN tool, the AM materials show similar profiles with an affected depth of ~ 30 μm, whereas the wrought material displays a deep compressive layer followed by tensile stresses, consistent with its higher hardness and tool‑wear‑induced instability.

A possible explanation for the resulting surface integrity effects is a combination of influences related to tool edge geometry, machining parameters and material properties of the tool as well as workpiece. The higher thermal conductivity of BL-CBN, compared to cemented carbide, leads to reduction in thermally induced degradation effects, thus, less tool wear. In addition, the BL-CBN tool has a less sharp cutting-edge geometry, with larger helix and rake angles, but machined at lower feed rate, leading to lower cutting forces and different effects on residual stresses in the workpiece surface.

sections.heading: Microstructural deformation mechanisms
paragraphs: The near‑surface microstructure after machining reveals distinct deformation mechanisms depending on material condition and tool type. The machined as‑built material shows grain refinement, with a slightly deeper affected zone for the BL‑CBN tool. This is consistent with its lower hardness and higher ductility [ 6 ,  22 ]. The HIP material exhibits deformation dominated by material drag, particularly for the CC tool. The heat‑treated material shows a shallow deformation zone combining material drag and grain refinement. These observations align with previous studies on the deformation behaviour for AM Alloy 718 [ 19 ,  20 ].

The observations correlate well with the FWHM results, as shown in Fig.  21 . The CC tool produces the lowest FWHM values in the as‑built and heat‑treated materials, indicating limited plastic deformation, while the wrought material shows the highest FWHM values. The BL‑CBN tool yields nearly identical FWHM profiles across all AM conditions, with a consistent affected depth of approximately 30 μm. The interpretation of FWHM as an indicator of plastic deformation and dislocation density is consistent with established methodology [ 30 ].

sections.heading: Future work
paragraphs: The results of the present study should be considered as an indication that further research and development is needed to adapt cutting conditions for optimal performance when machining AM Alloy 718. Additional work should also be carried out to verify the repeatability of the results. Although the results are clear and the explanations reasonable, the number of repetitions, number of samples, cutting lengths are limited.

It would be recommended to conduct a study with much longer cutting lengths to investigate how increased tool wear further influences the surface integrity. In such study, it would also be recommended to include surface integrity investigations of the wrought material to provide a robust reference.

It would also be interesting to investigate the effects of machining in the skin region, i.e., the outermost AM surface. The geometry analysis showed that the as-built state is prone to distort, whereas after HIP or heat-treatment the component geometry is improved. However, it may be difficult to determine the machining impact of the skin, as it is shallow, but it may induce a high impact on the tool edges as the skin have an alternating chemistry and microstructure.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study investigated the machining response and resulting surface integrity of additively manufactured (AM) Alloy 718 in three material conditions, as‑built, HIP, and heat‑treated, compared to conventional wrought Alloy 718, after machining with two tool concepts: a cemented carbide (CC) end mill and a binderless CBN (BL‑CBN) end mill. The study provides several new insights that advance the understanding of machining of AM Alloy 718, particularly regarding how microstructure governs machinability and the robustness of BL-CBN tools when machining AM Alloy 718. These insights are based on a comprehensive surface integrity characterisation that links surface roughness, residual stress profiles, and subsurface deformation mechanisms to microstructure and cutting tool concept. The aim has been to provide practical guidance for industry, with recommendations for tool selection and post-processing strategies when machining AM Alloy 718 components, as well as identifying further development needs.
On the basis of the investigations conducted, and considering their limitations, the following conclusions can be drawn:

Microstructure dictates machinability, as the AM material conditions exhibits distinct microstructures that directly influence hardness and deformation behaviour, thereby impacting the machining response. The BL-CBN tool concept provided superior and stable performance, as it consistently produced lower cutting forces, minimal wear, and uniform compressive stresses across all AM conditions. In contrast, the CC tool showed strong sensitivity to material condition and rapid wear progression. Surface integrity is strongly influenced by the tool concept, as the BL-CBN tool generates uniform surface roughness and compressive residual stresses, whereas the CC tool produces larger variations, especially for HIP and heat-treated materials. The tool concept and AM material condition govern the induced residual stresses, demonstrated by the BL-CBN tool producing consistent compressive stress levels (~ − 600 MPa) across AM conditions, whereas the CC tool generated larger variations, with the HIP material showing the highest compressive stresses. The wrought material exhibited the deepest stress penetration and, at long cutting lengths, transitioned to tensile stresses due to tool degradation. Subsurface deformation varies with microstructure and tool type, shown by the different deformation mechanisms observed for the AM materials. The as-built material shows grain refinement, the HIP material exhibits material drag, and the heat-treated material displayed a combination of drag and grain refinement. The BL-CBN tool produced shallower and more consistent deformation depths, while the CC tool caused deeper deformation in the HIP and wrought materials. The FWHM profiles confirm these trends, with the BL-CBN tool showing uniformly affected depths approximately 30 μm. Wrought Alloy 718 remains the most challenging material to machine, as it caused highest tool wear, deepest residual stresses and largest plastic deformation. The overall conclusion is that the BL-CBN is the preferred tool concept for machining AM Alloy 718 in this work, offering stable performance and superior surface integrity, independent of material condition. After implementation, it would improve productivity and decrease unwanted surface integrity effects when machining these types of alloys, for example within the aerospace industry. The results are promising but suggest that future work should investigate the repeatability of the findings and expand the parameter space for the selected materials.
